questions.q: What two conditions must a discrete probability distribution satisfy?
options: Every probability must be non-negative, and all probabilities must sum to exactly 1
Every probability must be exactly 0.5
There must be exactly two possible outcomes
All probabilities must be irrational numbers
questions.explain: A valid probability distribution requires non-negative probabilities that sum to 1 -- a qubit's P(0)=|alpha|^2 and P(1)=|beta|^2 satisfy this exactly because of the normalization condition.

questions.q: What is the formal definition of expectation value?
options: The sum of each possible outcome's value weighted by its probability: E[X] = sum of x times P(x)
The single most likely outcome
The average of outcomes actually observed in one specific experiment
The difference between the highest and lowest possible outcome values
questions.explain: Expectation value is a theoretical quantity defined from the probability distribution itself, not a count of what happened to be observed -- it's the probability-weighted average over all possible outcomes.

questions.q: In the worked example (P(0)=0.64, P(1)=0.36, using +1/-1 for outcomes 0/1), why is E[Z]=0.28 not equal to either +1 or -1?
options: Expectation value is a probability-weighted average across both possible outcomes, not a selection of one specific outcome -- it can land anywhere between the two possible values
The calculation in the example must contain an error
E[Z] should always equal exactly the more probable outcome's value
Expectation value is undefined whenever a distribution has more than one possible outcome
questions.explain: E[Z] = 0.64(+1) + 0.36(-1) = 0.28 is a weighted blend of both outcomes -- it's not meant to equal either individual outcome, just to reflect the distribution's overall lean.

questions.q: Why do quantum algorithms like VQE and QAOA typically care about the expectation value of an operator, rather than a single measurement outcome?
options: A single measurement is one noisy sample from the underlying distribution; the algorithm's math is built around the true expectation value, which only converges as more repeated measurements (shots) are taken
Single measurement outcomes are always identical to the expectation value, making the distinction irrelevant
Expectation values can only be computed classically, never from quantum measurements
These algorithms never actually use probability or measurement at all
questions.explain: One shot gives a random sample, not the expectation value itself -- these algorithms need the expectation value specifically, which requires averaging over many repeated runs of the circuit.

questions.q: Why does Qiskit (and similar tools) default to running a circuit many times (multiple shots) rather than just once?
options: Because a single shot only gives one random outcome from the distribution, while estimating an expectation value or the full distribution requires averaging over many repeated runs
Because running a circuit once is technically impossible on real hardware
Because multiple shots always produce the exact same result each time, so more shots just confirms correctness
Multiple shots are only needed when the circuit contains an error
questions.explain: Since each shot is one random sample from the probability distribution, only repeated sampling across many shots lets you estimate the true underlying distribution or its expectation value with reasonable confidence.
